sections.title: What is Interval DP?
sections.content:
**Interval DP** is a dynamic programming pattern where the subproblem is defined over a contiguous **interval** `[i, j]` - 'what is the optimal answer for the subarray, substring, or subsequence from index i to index j?' The recurrence splits this interval at some index k: `dp[i][j] = min/max over all k in [i, j-1] of (dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost(i, k, j))`. You build solutions for small intervals (length 1, then 2, then 3...) and combine them into larger ones.

This pattern is categorically different from 1D DP (one endpoint) and 2D DP on grids (two coordinates moving forward). In interval DP, both endpoints can vary and the recurrence looks backward into strictly smaller intervals - which is why you fill the table by **increasing interval length**, not by increasing i. The traversal order is non-obvious and getting it wrong produces wrong answers silently, because `dp[i][j]` is computed before the sub-intervals it depends on are ready.

Classic problems: **Matrix Chain Multiplication** (minimize scalar multiplications to compute a chain of matrix products), **Burst Balloons** (choose the order to pop balloons for maximum coins - the last balloon popped in a range is the split point), **Strange Printer** (minimum turns to print a string), **Palindrome Partitioning II** (minimum cuts to partition into palindromes), and **Minimum Cost to Merge Stones**. All share the same shape: split an interval at k, solve both halves recursively, combine.

The time complexity is always O(n³) in the standard form - O(n²) states times O(n) choices for the split point k. Space is O(n²) for the DP table. For n up to ~500 this is fast enough. For n up to ~1000 it becomes borderline. When you see n ≤ 500 and the problem involves some 'optimal order of operations' on a sequence, interval DP is almost certainly the intended solution.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use interval DP when the problem asks for an optimal way to split, merge, or operate on a sequence, and the cost of operating on a range depends on how you split it. The hallmark: the problem asks for the best 'order of operations' on a sequence - and changing the order changes the total cost. If choosing which element to process last in a range makes subproblems independent, interval DP applies.
signals: minimum cost to split or merge sequence
optimal order of operations on array

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
## Table Fill Order

Fill by interval **length**, not by row. The correct loop structure:

```
for (let len = 2; len <= n; len++):         // interval length
  for (let i = 0; i <= n - len; i++):       // left endpoint
    let j = i + len - 1;                    // right endpoint
    for (let k = i; k < j; k++):            // split point
      dp[i][j] = optimal(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost)
```

This guarantees that when computing `dp[i][j]`, all `dp[i][k]` and `dp[k+1][j]` for strictly smaller intervals are already computed. Base case: set `dp[i][i]` for all i (single-element intervals) before the length loop.

**Never fill by row first** - `dp[0][3]` needs `dp[1][3]` which needs `dp[2][3]`, so row-first order computes large intervals before the smaller ones they depend on.

## Matrix Chain Multiplication

Given matrices A1...An where Ai has dimensions `p[i-1] × p[i]`, minimize total scalar multiplications to compute the product. `dp[i][j]` = minimum multiplications for matrices i through j. Split at k: cost is `dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i-1] * p[k] * p[j]`. Base case: `dp[i][i] = 0` (single matrix, no multiplication needed). This is the canonical interval DP problem.

## Burst Balloons - The "Last to Pop" Reframe

Given balloons with values, popping balloon i when its neighbors are l and r gives `nums[l] * nums[i] * nums[r]` coins. Goal: maximize total coins.

**Key reframe**: instead of which balloon to pop FIRST (order-dependent, subproblems aren't independent), think which balloon to pop **LAST** in range `[i, j]`. `dp[i][j]` = max coins from popping all balloons strictly between i and j. If k is the last balloon popped: `dp[i][j] = max over k of (dp[i][k] + nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j] + dp[k][j])` for k from i+1 to j-1.

Add sentinel balloons with value 1 at both ends to handle boundaries. The 'last to pop' reframe makes subproblems independent - when k is the last balloon in [i,j] to pop, balloons in [i,k] and [k,j] have already been fully popped and don't interfere.

## Palindrome Partitioning + String Interval DP

For minimum cuts to partition `s` into palindromes: pre-build a 2D `isPalin[i][j]` boolean table using interval DP (expand from single chars and pairs outward). Then run a 1D DP `cuts[j]` = minimum cuts for `s[0..j]`: for each j, try all i from 0 to j where `isPalin[i][j]` is true, take `cuts[j] = min(cuts[i-1] + 1)`. This chains two DP computations: the palindrome table first, then the partition DP.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Fills the DP table by interval length (outer loop), ensuring all sub-interval answers are ready before combining. Split point k tries every way to divide [i, j] into two subproblems.

items.name: Burst Balloons
items.description: Reframe as 'which balloon to pop last in [i, j]' instead of first - this makes subproblems independent. Add sentinel values of 1 at both ends of the array. dp[i][j] = max coins popping all balloons strictly between i and j.

items.name: Strange Printer
items.description: Minimum print turns for a string. If `s[i] === s[j]`, the last character can be printed in the same turn as s[i], so `dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-1]`. Otherwise try all splits k and take the min of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j].

items.name: Minimum Cost to Merge Stones
items.description: Merge adjacent groups of k piles into one; only valid splits exist when `(j - i) % (k - 1) === 0`. Interval DP with a constraint on valid split points - tests recognizing when not all k values produce valid sub-intervals.

items.name: Palindrome Partitioning II
items.description: Chain two DP computations: first build the isPalin[i][j] table using interval DP in O(n²), then run a 1D minimum-cuts DP using the palindrome table. Tests composing two DP solutions where the output of one feeds into the other.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.explanation: There are O(n²) intervals [i, j] and for each, O(n) choices for the split point k - total O(n³) time. The DP table stores one value per interval: O(n²) space. For n = 500, O(n³) = 125M operations - tight but feasible within typical time limits. For n = 1000 it becomes 10^9 operations and likely TLEs without optimizations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Wrong fill order - filling by row (outer loop i, inner loop j) computes dp[i][j] before smaller intervals like dp[i+1][j] and dp[i][j-1] are ready, causing the algorithm to read uninitialized zero values and produce silently wrong results.

Base case off-by-one - `dp[i][i]` must be initialized to its correct value (usually 0) before the length loop starts; leaving them as the default zero when zero is not the correct base value causes wrong results for all length-2 intervals that depend on them.

Wrong split range for k - k should run from `i` to `j-1` inclusive for most problems; shifting to `i+1` to `j` or `i` to `j` creates split points where one sub-interval is empty or the other overlaps the boundary, producing incorrect sub-problems.

Burst Balloons: thinking which balloon to pop FIRST instead of LAST - the 'first to pop' framing makes sub-problems depend on each other because popping a balloon changes the neighbors of its former neighbors; only 'last to pop' produces truly independent sub-intervals.

Not adding sentinel values in Burst Balloons - without the sentinel 1s at both ends of `nums`, balloons at the boundary have undefined left or right neighbors during the cost calculation, causing index-out-of-bounds errors or incorrect coin values at the edges.

items.title: Burst Balloons
items.why: Tests the 'last to pop' reframe that makes sub-problems independent, sentinel boundary values, and correct interval DP fill order - the canonical hard interval DP problem.

items.title: Strange Printer
items.why: Tests the special case `s[i] === s[j]` that collapses the cost, and the general split-point recurrence for minimum-operations interval DP.

items.title: Minimum Cost to Merge Stones
items.why: Tests interval DP with a validity constraint on split points - only splits where `(j - i) % (k - 1) === 0` are valid, requiring an extra feasibility check inside the k loop.

items.title: Palindrome Partitioning II
items.why: Tests chaining two DP computations - palindrome table (interval DP) followed by minimum-cuts DP - and recognizing when a 2D precomputed structure feeds into a 1D DP.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Interval DP defines subproblems over two endpoints [i, j] with O(n³) complexity. LIS returns to single-endpoint DP but introduces a completely different optimization: the O(n log n) patience sorting solution using binary search on a tails array - a different algorithmic lever from anything in interval DP.
